blocks.x: We usually make a note on this tape so we know what it is. Let me put this down first. This is an interview with Mr. Lee Page. What is the address here? 121 North Dugan Way.
I'm going to do that.
Start the debut on WDSU TV. Y'all alternate in talking and I can talk better. All righty. First, let me poke words at me and I'll...
Okay, it's going all right.
All right, Lee, would you tell a little bit about your debut in TV here in New Orleans?

Yes, when I made my debut was here in New Orleans over WDSU, Channel 6 on Royal Street and the 400 block here in New Orleans. I appeared there for quite some time after making my debut. And at that time, the manager of the station was Live Right, which we call him Mr. X now.
Lee, how about Channel 14 in Evansville where they were... Oh, yes.

...ripping your accent? Well, I was appearing on Channel 6, that's Channel... 14. ...14 in Evansville. And they were interviewing me and they were talking about my southern accent. So they kept going on about it and said, you really have a southern accent? And I said, well, is there any other way to talk?
And then how about, Lee, when you were in St. Louis singing on WIL radio and the... and the new song that came out, My Handyman? Oh, yes.

When I was appearing on WIL in St. Louis, Missouri there, and the staff there as a vocalist, well, the song came out, a real popular number and new number. And that's why I was keeping up with the new tunes and it's called My Handyman. So I got the song and learned it and went down to the radio station and went on the air and I was starting off to sing it. And I got about eight bars of the song and they cut me off the air. They announced it, I hollered back there, get another song, we can't have that one on the air. They called it Risgué. So then a week later, well, everybody in St. Louis and all the radio stations was singing it.
Ethel Waters, they've made a record of it. Yes, Ethel Waters. He can tell you about it. Would those be similar words as the ones you were using or were yours? No, this was on the sheet music.
It was right in the sheet music.
Right in the sheet music. Well, what she's using is in the sheet music too. Bill.

Yes. Yeah, I know Ethel Waters and, you know, Ethel Waters has been around quite a long time. She used to do some coon shouting too, you know. Back in 1918, when she recorded the song in 1918, there'll be some changes made on Black Bird Recording Company. In 1918, she was doing coon shouting for this Black Bird Recording Company. What was that?
Black Swan, I believe.
No, Black Bird. Black Bird? Black Bird Recording Company.
I have some of the old records that are on the label called Black Swan.
I know, Black Bird. And there'll be some changes made back in 1918.
Lee, how about Prohibition in Chicago? Oh, yes.

During my time of show business and back in the Prohibition days, I appeared at the various nightclubs there. And I happened to be appearing at the Triangle nightclub there, which at that time was one of the popular nightclubs. And the very well-known gentleman owned the place was Al Capone. And I was working for him, and there was a very successful engagement. And he had a lot of nice people working for him there, but he had some people working for him. It kind of took a liking to me, but I was a little bit afraid of him.
Would you like to tell a little bit more about Henderson? Can you tell us about some of the, when you were back there a few years ago when they made it Leapage Day? Yes.

Well, about a couple of years ago I was back in Henderson, Kentucky, visiting there. And that's the first time I had been back there in quite some time. And they declared the one day there as Leapage Day. I was honorary mayor and chief of police and city officials for the one day there. And it was quite a big affair, and I was interviewed by the newspapers there and had pictures all over the paper. And I was quite flattered and honored.
How about the editor, Lee, of the local newspaper there that thought perhaps you needed some protection? Oh, yes.

While I was there walking down the street, which I usually do, have my bodyguard with me on these tours and things in Henderson. Well, I didn't take any bodyguard along. I was walking down the street and I met one of the reporters and editor of the local newspaper there, the Journal. And they greeted me on the street and stopped me and said to me, he said, Lee, where's your bodyguard? You walking around by yourself? I said, well, I shouldn't have to have no bodyguard in Henderson. This is my own hometown.
Lee, would you tell a little bit how you, when you were a boy at home, how you watched the hired hands, the colored held hands?

Oh, yes. On the plantation in Kentucky when I was a boy. I was born and raised in a plantation in Kentucky. We had help working around our hired hands. And I used to watch the colored people jump around and dance and sing. And I learned a lot by just watching the hired hands and I'd get ideas from them. And when I was quite a small child, I remember my brother, Richard, he and his buddy came home one day and they wanted me to sing. And I don't, I was so small, I don't remember ever singing. I didn't know what I was going to sing. So they offered me a nickel to sing and I wouldn't take it. So they offered me a dime and I wouldn't take it. So they offered me a quarter and I don't know whether I sing or not. I'm too little, I was too little, I don't remember that part.
Lee, after you left Ned Waver and the Foundation of Singing and Dancing School, didn't you play at New York at the corporate band and Latin Quarters?

Oh, yes. After taking up the foundation of dancing and everything, the basics of all of it and singing, well then I worked at some of their leading nightclubs there such as the Coke Cabana and the Latin Quarters there, which at that time was two of their most popular nightclubs.
How about Robert Elton and the Missouri Rockets lead?

Oh, yes. That was quite a memorable time. I remember I worked as a course boy. There was twelve of us fellas and eighteen girls in a line, the original Missouri Rockets from the Missouri Theatre in St. Louis, Missouri. And we went from the St. Louis, Missouri, the Missouri Theatre to the Roxy Theatre in New York. Then I left them and went then as an individual singer and dancer.
And then later on, Lee, didn't you work with Mary Martin, Ginger Rogers and Helen Morgan?

Yes, Mary Martin played in the Broadway show, Louisiana Hayride and also Hollywood Follies. And these other people, I worked with Helen Morgan, too, several times in nightclubs and also taught a girl who went with her show as a course girl.
How about Connie Boswell and Ella Mae Morris?
Yes, Connie Boswell is a dear friend of mine and I knew the Boswell sisters, Connie, Martha and Bette. They're girls from New Orleans.
They came from over in Isle of Jairs across the river, isn't it?
Yes, that's right. And they were very fine singers. I knew them well. Been known them for years. I worked on the show with Connie Boswell, Hattie Call show. We traveled all over the country.
Oh yeah, what about that show? They finally folded up, didn't it?

Yeah, they folded up the, well they didn't fold up the Hattie Call, now they got a new drug out and it's in pill form called the New Hattie Call. Oh really? I didn't know. Oh yes, oh yes, oh yes, it's still going. I didn't know what happened to it. No, it's still going. The show folded up, but we traveled all over the country with that and I worked with Connie Boswell.
Was Sharky on that show? Do you remember?
He was on there for a while and they changed bands with it, see.
And remember any other musicians on that show from here?

No, I don't remember too many of them. I remember Connie Boswell, who were very good friends and I know her sisters too. You know, one of her sisters has a turkey farm up north. Oh, is there? Oh yes, and the other one passed on. Yeah. Yeah, one of them has a turkey farm.
Lee, how about the woman pianist in the Chicago speak that told you not to change her style?

Oh yes, I was a guest at one of the cocktail lounges in Chicago many years ago and there was a colored girl playing the piano there, a very fine piano player. And they asked me to get up as a guest and do a number, which I was called on. And she told me to never change my style for nobody. And I had a different style and something good and unusual for me to stick with it.
Lee, didn't you work with Mae West? That's the mess. And wasn't her husband from your hometown of Kentucky?

Yes, Mae West, I worked with her and her husband is from Henderson, Kentucky. And she appeared in Henderson before my time, but I was told by my father that she appeared in Henderson back in 1909. Oh for heaven's sakes. With the show there and she had all men in the show but the maid. She never has no women in her show, only the maid. And back in 1909 she got arrested for a risque show.
Lee, how about that old spiel that she used about come up and see me sometime?

Oh yes, I always get a kick out of Mae West when she always says, come up and see me sometime. So I was appearing in a show with her and she was going on that and she said to me, she said, well, why don't you come up and see me sometime? I said, well, Mae, I can't come up and see you. She said, why? I said, well, I'm a coon shouter and I'd be shouting too loud.
And then did Mae give any comment to that, peel me a grape?
Oh, she says, oh, peel me a grape.
Oh, Lee, didn't you at one time, weren't you the only person that ever performed a male striptease for ladies' club?

Yes. Back in about 49, well, I was in a Grover La Rose theatrical booking agency's office in St. Louis, Missouri. And during the time I was in his office, he had a phone call and it was a ladies' club that called up and they wanted something unusual and different. And they specified they'd like a male strip dancer. They asked the agent if there was such a thing as a strip dancer. So he turns around to me and joking and said to me, he said, how would you like to be a strip dancer? And I said, well, if there's any money in it, I'm interested. So he said, well, there's a lady on the phone who wants a male strip dancer. And it's a ladies' organization of about 500 to 1,000 women. So I took the job as a male strip dancer and appeared at this club there for all women's audience from 500 to 1,000 women from all the leading hotels in St. Louis as a male strip dancer.
Lee, how did these ladies react? Didn't you come, didn't you wear formal clothes or something? How was their reaction?

Well, I dressed as I was going to a semi-formal with the tux trousers and the white coat and all the paraphernalia that goes with it. And they react to a man's strip dancer as the men act to ladies' strip dancers.
Lee, how about the Freedom Train show?

Well, that was quite an experience that I had. I traveled with the Freedom Train show and I appeared here in New Orleans, Memphis, and St. Louis. And in St. Louis, I was very well received there on the banks of the Mississippi River where I appeared. I was only scheduled to do three songs and a dance. And I was so successful at the three songs and a dance. I had to do six songs and three dances that liked to kill me. The Post-Dispatch paper there wrote me up and said that I was the only one that woke the people up in St. Louis that could hear me coon shouting for 15 blocks. I was backed up by Russ Davis, KMOX, Augusta.
Lee, didn't you play with Martha Ray a number of years ago at the Oriental Theater?

Yes, I remember Martha Ray in Chicago at the Oriental Theater there. I worked on the bill there with her. And I got a huge kick out of her with the way she would stretch her mouth and the way she would shake when she was going off the stage.
Well, I was going to ask some more about Mae West. If you remember, did she ever appear in New Orleans much or ever worked down here?
As I know of, Mae West never did appear in New Orleans to my knowledge.
They made a movie that was supposed to be based on Basin Street.
Yes, but the scenes were not of New Orleans.
No, I thought I wondered if she'd ever had any experience here.
As far as I know, no. She's never been in New Orleans. I knew anything about her. I never heard her mention New Orleans at all. But she's been to all the other cities. I was quite surprised.
Lee, at one time or other, didn't you have Clyde McCoy play with you?
Yes, I appeared with Clyde McCoy in quite a number of places. Some of them were in ballrooms and some of them were in nightclubs, supper clubs.
Lee, didn't you also work in some walkathons in Chicago?

Yes, I appeared at the Coliseum there to over 75,000. I took a show from the Club Vista nightclub at 47th and Cottage Grove where I was appearing. And was very well received and they got a huge kick out of my coon shouting.
Tell about how the people drug themselves.

Oh, and I was appearing there and the people, actually it was a walkathon. And I got a kick out of the way they were dragging one another around either by the hair or the head or by their heels or the arms or any way they could drag them around. One would be asleep and the other would be dragging him around or he'd be out from desolation.
Didn't the manager of the Coliseum, the owner, call up your manager at the Club Vista at the time?

Yes, when I got back to the Club Vista, well they had a various number of calls and the manager had also called from the walkathon and told my boss what a wonderful show that I put on and how I was received.
What were some of the songs you sang around then? What, Coconut Island or were some of those around, was that popular around that time?
Well, at that show that night I sang I Can't Dance and was popular and on the Coconut Island and Stay Away from Dixieland.
Ah, Lee, who was in your hometown there in Henderson, weren't there? Some red light districts. I know they had, didn't they have a place called Audubon, Sally Smith Heart?
Ah, yes, it was a place there called Sally Smith Hearts. It was out in Audubon, in the East End. It was quite a notorious place and quite an exclusive place, you know.
Ah, didn't, did they have a player piano?

Yeah, they had an old player piano. You put a nickel in the, oh yeah. Then what I would get a kick out of, if you would go by there, well you would see the women with their bare legs sticking out the window shaking them all like, Ah, you boys!
Wasn't there some sort of a tradition they used to say about Sally and her best, and the best customers in the house?
Well, yes, I just don't recall just how that phrase went.
All right. Lee, didn't you also play at the World's Fair in 1933?

Yeah, I appeared there with Sally Rand and Sally Rand's show in 1933, and her show, and the streets of Paris, and all of that business about Sally Rand getting arrested every day, that was publicity. She did, but she didn't. That was publicity. Without Sally Rand there would have been no fair. And in 1934, the second year, I appeared on the Midway in the Rumba show. I was the only Rumba dancer. I went from coon shouting and tap dancing to a Rumba dancer.
Lee, didn't you also invent a few dances?

Well, yes, shortly after the Second World War, well I created a dance called the Peace Time Hop. The reason I called it the Peace Time Hop, going from wartime to peace, I thought it would be very appropriate at that time to call it Peace Time Hop, which became very popular in the East Coast and in the West.
How about the Jeep, Lee?

Well, the Jeep is a dance that I did when I was peering in Chicago, so long around there. And also another dance that I did in Chicago during that time called the Palsy Walk, which was quite the thing in Chicago.
What was the, excuse me for interrupting, what was the Jeep live, Suzy?
Well, it was something on the order of the Suzy Q and trucking, and same way by the palsy, only you would shake your head and shake all over, it's like you had the palsy.
Lee, didn't you also design some clothes for men?

Yes, I designed a suit shortly after the Second World War, when the ladies' styles came out with the long skirts and dresses. Well, I figured the men should have something keeping in trend with the women, so I designed a suit called the New Look Suit for Men, which was in Look Magazine and Life Magazine, and was made in New Orleans and in St. Louis.
Lee, didn't, weren't there pictures of it in Look Magazine and some of the radios and other newspapers?
Yes, it was in Look Magazine and was also very frequently discussed on radio at that time about the New Look Suit for Men.
What was the cut of the suit? What did it look like?

Well, it was a very trim suit and had the, I'll say a long coat, not too long, but long enough, and it had a removable belt. The belt went all the way around. You could wear it as a sport coat with the belt, or you could remove the belt and wear it as a dress coat.
Lee, in the 40's, didn't you appear here at Abilene, Texas? You were in a USO tour show or something, you went through hell and high water to get a roof over your head.

Yes, I remember that. I like to froze to death. We were appearing at the army camp in Abilene, Texas, and it was 15 below zero and snow about knee deep. And when we arrived there, well, there was no place for us to stay as the army camp was overcrowded. The town was about 40,000 population and there was about 80,000 people trying to live there and there was no place to stay. So we had to set up in the bus stations at night and sleep the best we could and go hungry in the daytime because all the food and everything was ate up.
Lee, weren't there some other people featured in the act? There was some they didn't give a very good response. Weren't there jugglers?

Oh yes, I remember this time in our show we had a very fine juggler and had a very fine act and very nice gentleman. He was about 25 years old and he always went on before I did. And he had an exceptionally good act. He was a juggler. But when he would go on the stage for some unknown reason at all, they would heckle him and hiss him and tell him he was in the wrong uniform and everything. And had me quite frightened that I had to follow someone like that. But it never happened to me. They always screamed and hollered and applauded for my style of singing, which had proved that coon shouting is accepted any place in the United States.
I was going to ask some more about if there's anything else you can tell about the coon shouting style. I mean is it usually pretty loud or is it a part of it?

Well, a coon shouting, no that's where so many people gets confused. They think you have to sing so loud it isn't the loudness. It's the type of voice you have and the style of singing you do and the feeling you put in the song or in the words. And you must pronounce your words very distinctly and put some feeling to them, not just mumble them. As I imagine you noticed in some of my write-ups there that I'm the only singer that doesn't mumble. Yeah, I've heard of that. Or groan or sneeze or sniff or moan or groan or do something. And that's one of the characteristics of coon shouting. You must pronounce your words distinctly. You must have a solid beat and not give up your beat. Just keep stomping and shouting and keep going. And you don't wait for nothing. The musician's got to keep up with you.
Lee, during the 40's what were the name of some of the jazz blues and boogie woogie numbers you sang?
Well, some of the boogie woogie numbers was Cow Cow Boogie and Pig Foot Pete and Beat Me Daddy Eight to the Bar and Scrubbing Me Mama with a Boogie Brush and numbers of that sort.
Lee, didn't you used to listen a lot? Weren't you influenced quite a bit by the records of Bessie Smith and also Fats Waller? Did you used to hear Fats sing?

Oh yes, I have quite a bit of his records and I always liked his style of singing and I think he was a wonderful piano player. I liked his style of playing and his style of singing. I do a lot of his numbers called Why Am I Neglected and Honey Keep Your Mind On Me and Honeysuckle Rose and all those numbers that he did. I liked his style. And Bessie Smith, I do her first number that she ever recorded. I have the original music on it and I sing it. It's called Golf Coast Blues, which is a popular number today and it's one of Bessie Smith's first recordings. And I guess I'm the only singer today that sings it. And I do it in coon shouting.
Lee, isn't there another one you added in your repertoire by Bessie Smith about the sea diver?

Oh yeah, I do her number called Mr. Deep Sea Diver, which is a blues tune with parodies to it and breaks. You can take most any song and do it in coon shouting. Just say we'll just use the blues. We'll just say like Memphis blues or anything. Well you take it and you sing about eight bars and you put a break in it or any blues and break it up like that. And you can do it in coon shouting or any blues. No worries. You can take any jazz tune. Just like in Way Down Yonor New Orleans and that part, stop, give your lady fair a little smile. Stop, da da da da. Well, it's a real coon shouting type of a number. If you've noticed, so many of the singers that sing that actually don't sing it like it's written.
Lee, didn't you often attend minstrel shows and weren't you in blackface too?

Oh yes, I did blackface, not so much of the minstrel shows as I worked all over the country in theaters and nightclubs as a blackface act. And it's not a minstrel act, it's entirely different in a minstrel. Minstrel, you know, they paint around their lips white and in red blackface you don't do that. You make yourself black all over and leave your lips naturally.
Do you remember any early minstrel shows when you were a kid, very young, what they were like up in Kentucky? Do you remember any traveling shows going through there?
Oh, I can't remember the name of them but I can remember what they looked like and I used to go to see all of them. And Penrose is one of them. He used to have a blackface act out on Penrose.

Did any colored minstrel shows, I understand they have both colored and white minstrel shows in those days. Do you remember seeing ads, even if you didn't go to any colored minstrel shows, do you remember seeing any ads for them up there?
No, as far as I know, the colored minstrels didn't come to Kentucky.
I think Handy says he was with one of them for a while in later years. I just wondered if...
Well, I don't think they come to Henderson if they did, that's beyond my knowledge. I don't know anything about it. They might have, but I doubt that.
Do you remember any of the early Coonschauters that were typical of that style, people that might have made records?

No, the ones that I know and I used to see and would do that style or any ways near that, I don't know if they ever made records. If they did, I didn't know anything about it. But I did hear some when I was a very small kid singing. The fact about it, when I was a small kid, I never heard nobody sing any other way. That was a popular song. That was a popular way. And I'm the only singer today, as they tell me, that is a Coonschauter. As Sophie Tucker says, she's the last of the Red Hot Mamas, but I'm the last of the Coonschauters. I'm the modern singer of today that sings like they did during the Civil War, which is considered unusual and different. I'm the last one at sings like that, which is a style of singing during the Civil War back in the 18's.
Lee, at one time when you were in blackface, didn't you have an embarrassing experience with the cork when you were in?

Oh yes, when I first started doing blackface naturally, I didn't know anything about putting the blackface on, the cork and all this stuff. And the fact about it, it wasn't exactly a cork. I think it was a little cork and grease mixed up together. And I put it on and went out and did the dance and got to perspiring and it all just run off. And I looked like one of these Georgia watermelons.
Lee, weren't you also influenced a lot by some of Ethel Waters' recordings? Wasn't there one of her numbers that you have done, you've added in your repertoire? Or a couple of them?

I think that I did quite a few Ethel Waters' numbers. I did one that she recorded and it's very popular and I did it quite frequently. And it's the blues tune, Stormy Weather, which is a very popular blues and it's a good coon shouting number. And on those type of numbers, I also do the original number of Pray For The Light To Go Out. I have the original music on it. I have the music there too. And it's quite popular. It also takes a long tug out and makes a preacher lay the Bible down. And all those type of numbers. And I do all popular tunes today. I take all these popular numbers and sing them. I have no difficulties in singing the popular tunes because it's the way you sing and the type of voice you've got. You can take any number and do it that way. And what they're doing today too is they're taking these popular blues that's written slow and picking the tempo up. They're taking the ones that's written fast and slowing them down and call them new tunes.
Lee, when you first started in show business, didn't you work for a dollar and a half or a couple or two dollars or something like that? What were the wages?
Well, when I started out, a dollar and a half a night was top salary. And when you got twenty-five dollars a week, well, you were a headliner.
Lee, also wasn't your voice so clear and loud on certain occasions, for example, like at the Grand Theatre in St. Louis, where they didn't need a microphone for you?

Oh, yes. I was appearing there back in 1948, I believe, or 49, somewhere along that area. I was appearing to Grand Theatre in St. Louis, the burlesque show at 6th and Market Street in St. Louis, Missouri. And Mr. Zeissler was the owner there. And I was appearing there as a song and dance act. And they had a microphone there, and naturally I was using the mic as usual. And they came back and took the microphone away from me. And they told me I was the first singer that had been in there in fifteen years that didn't have to have a microphone. They said I was deafening the people in the back with a microphone, and they could hear me just as plain without it as if they were sitting in the front row.
We have about a minute left on this tape. I wonder if we can finish up on this. If there's anything else about the New Orleans musicians, or just the scene here in general, that you'd like to add?

Well, the musicians here are very capable. The local musicians playing for my style of singing, because they play that type of music. And they've got a lot of very fine, good musicians here that plays all this jazz and stuff. Like the Dukes of Dixieland and Sharky and all of them, they can play all that type of music.
Can you tell, Lee, how the name originated, your title, Mr. Bourbon Street?

Well, yes, because I'm from this part of the country and from the south where all this jazz and blues originated. And every place I go, well, they always refer to me as Mr. Bourbon Street himself. And my Dixieland jazz and blues and coon shouting and my flash and rhythm tap dancing. Which, it's an unusual style and something new and different in this area from the Civil War days, but it's modern today, a hundred years later.
Didn't the three newspapers at one time in New Orleans, Lee, verify that everyone on Bourbon Street knew you?

Oh, yes. I remember walking down Bourbon Street with three of the newspaper reporters, the States and Adam and the other newspaper they had here at that time. And everybody, when I was going down the street with them, everybody was hollering at me. The shoeshine boys, the garbage men, the nightclub owners and the show girls and show people were all hollering at me. And they made a statement at, they had been on the newspaper for fifteen years and that they had never walked down the street with anybody that was as well known as I was. Everybody was hollering at me like that.
Lee, how about Hoagie Carmichael?

Oh, yeah. Hoagie Carmichael. He is from Terre Haute, Indiana. It's his home. And I was appearing at one of the nightclubs there. And a funny incident happened. And after we finished our show, we went over to the club where he happened to be in. He wasn't playing there, but he was in there. And we didn't know it. And we walked in. There was an Augusta playing. And a piano player playing there. And just regular music was going. And people were just talking and drinking and dancing. And we weren't paying any attention. So somebody at the next table. So somebody at the next table, I heard him say to someone else, who's that playing that piano up there? And somebody very casual said, oh, that's homie Carmichael. Just like he was nobody.
Lee, didn't you play a lot in D.C.? Weren't you at the Chanticleer nightclub?
The Chanticleer is in Baltimore. And I played it to Tradewinds in Washington, D.C. And a Chanticleer in Washington, D.C. at 14th and K.
I see. Lee, wasn't there one club you worked at? It was a gambling place and they broke it up. And then it was back in full swing.
Mm-hm.

segments.title: Debut on WDSU TV in New Orleans and Evansville accent story
segments.summary: Paige describes his television debut on WDSU Channel 6 and an Evansville interview about his southern accent.

segments.title: 'My Handyman' cut off the air in St. Louis; Ethel Waters and coon shouting
segments.summary: On WIL in St. Louis he was cut off for singing 'My Handyman'; talk of Ethel Waters's recording and her 1918 label.

segments.title: Prohibition-era Chicago: working for Al Capone at the Triangle
segments.summary: He played the Triangle nightclub in Chicago, owned by Al Capone.

segments.title: Leapage Day in Henderson, Kentucky
segments.summary: He was honorary mayor for a day in his hometown and joked with a newspaper editor about his bodyguard.

segments.title: Boyhood on a Kentucky plantation watching hired hands
segments.summary: He learned singing and dancing by watching Black farm hands, and recalls his brother Richard offering him money to sing.

segments.title: New York nightclubs and the Missouri Rockets chorus line
segments.summary: After dance and singing training he played New York clubs and was a chorus boy with the Missouri Rockets.

segments.title: Working with Mary Martin and Helen Morgan
segments.summary: He recalls Mary Martin's Broadway shows and nightclub work with Helen Morgan.

segments.title: Connie Boswell and the Hadacol show
segments.summary: He knew the Boswell sisters from New Orleans and toured with Connie Boswell on a sponsored show.

segments.summary: A Black woman pianist at a Chicago lounge advised him to keep his own style.

segments.title: Mae West and her Henderson connection
segments.summary: He worked with Mae West, relays her Henderson visit in 1909, and tells the 'come up and see me' joke.

segments.title: Performing as a male stripper for a St. Louis ladies' club
segments.summary: Booked through Grover La Rose's agency, he did a male strip act for a women's audience.

segments.title: The Freedom Train show
segments.summary: He toured with the Freedom Train show in New Orleans, Memphis and St. Louis, where he was a hit.

segments.summary: He shared a Chicago bill with Martha Raye; the interviewer asks if Mae West ever worked New Orleans.

segments.title: Clyde McCoy and the Chicago walkathon
segments.summary: He appeared with Clyde McCoy and performed at a Coliseum walkathon, describing contestants and songs sung.

segments.title: Red-light places in Henderson
segments.summary: He recalls Sally Smith's house in Audubon and its player piano.

segments.title: Sally Rand and the 1933-34 World's Fair
segments.summary: He appeared with Sally Rand's show in 1933 and as a rumba dancer in 1934.

segments.title: Dances he created: Peace Time Hop, Jeep, Palsy Walk
segments.summary: He describes dances he invented after World War II and in Chicago.

segments.title: Designing the New Look Suit for Men
segments.summary: He designed a men's suit featured in Look and Life, and describes its cut.

segments.title: USO show in freezing Abilene, Texas
segments.summary: On a USO tour at an Abilene army camp there was no lodging in snow; a juggler was heckled.

segments.title: What coon shouting is and boogie-woogie numbers
segments.summary: He explains that coon shouting is about distinct diction and a solid beat, and lists boogie numbers he sang.

segments.title: Fats Waller and Bessie Smith in his repertoire
segments.summary: He sings Fats Waller and Bessie Smith numbers and says any blues or jazz tune can be done as coon shouting.

segments.title: Blackface, minstrel shows and being the last coon shouter
segments.summary: He distinguishes blackface from minstrelsy, recalls Kentucky shows, and calls himself the last coon shouter.

segments.title: Ethel Waters numbers he sings
segments.summary: He sings Ethel Waters's 'Stormy Weather' and others and comments on tempo changes in popular tunes.

segments.title: Early wages in show business
segments.summary: A dollar and a half a night was top pay and twenty-five dollars a week made you a headliner.

segments.title: Singing without a microphone at the Grand Theatre in St. Louis
segments.summary: At a St. Louis burlesque house he was the first singer in fifteen years who did not need a microphone.

segments.title: New Orleans musicians
segments.summary: He praises local musicians such as the Dukes of Dixieland for backing his style.

segments.title: Origin of the name 'Mr. Bourbon Street'
segments.summary: He explains his nickname and a walk down Bourbon Street with newspaper reporters.

segments.title: Hoagy Carmichael in Terre Haute
segments.summary: He tells of walking into a club where Hoagy Carmichael was casually playing piano.

segments.title: Chanticleer and Tradewinds clubs; closing
segments.summary: He clarifies where he played the Chanticleer and Tradewinds; the tape ends on a gambling club question.
